papers.title: The Self-Improvement Problem
papers.first_page: The Self-Improvement Problem Brian B. Moser1,2 , Stanislav Frolov1 , Tobias C. Nauen1,2 , Federico Raue1 , Andreas Dengel1,2 1 German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI) 2 RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau first.last@dfki.de Abstract arXiv:2610.21646v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026 With the rise of large language models, agentic systems are becoming increasingly autonomous, as they write code, call tools, revise prompts, and propose modifications to their own components. This autonomy raises a fundamental question for safe self-improvement: can an automated gate like a reward model or an automated reviewer reliably decide whether a proposed update should be accepted? The difficulty is structural. The gate must be a terminating, computable procedure, while the property we ultimately care about, namely whether an update is a genuine semantic improvement, depends on potentially unbounded program behavior. We formalize this mismatch by modeling agents as programs and defining improvement in terms of a semantic score that need not be computable. We study two evaluation abstractions. The first is a certifier that approves or rejects an update. The second is a search procedure that, given access to a proposal generator, attempts to output some improving candidate if one exists. We show that, in the fully general setting, no terminating procedure can simultaneously guarantee reliability (never accepting a non-improvement) and non-conservatism (never missing an available improvement): self-referential constructions can force any such gate or searcher to fail. Randomized gates with bounded error face the same limit. We then identify a standard decidable regime used in practice (bounded evaluation and a finite proposal budget) under which exhaustive simulation yields a terminating search procedure with the desired guarantees. We also show the limit of this recovery: a chain of accepted updates can raise the bounded score in every round while the true score falls. Our results draw a boundary between unbounded, universal settings where correctness guarantees collapse and bounded settings where they can be recovered by design. 1 Introduction Many modern “agentic” pipelines follow the same pattern: an agent proposes a self-update (a code patch, prompt rewrite, new checkpoint, tool policy, etc.), and an automated gate decides whether to apply it (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025). The gate may be a reward model, a regression test suite, or an automated reviewer that must terminate and output accept/reject. The intended notion of improvement, however, is semantic: whether the updated agent is genuinely better depends on unbounded program behavior, long-horizon interactions, and open-ended tool use (Wang et al., 2023). This mismatch creates a concrete failure mode that is now routine in practice: once the proposal mechanism can anticipate or condition on the gate, it can “optimize the gate” rather than the intended objective. In other words, the proposer can exploit the evaluator as a predictable part of the environment. This paper formalizes that failure mode and proves a sharp boundary: in a fully general setting, no terminating gate or search procedure can be both reliable and non-conservative. The core obstruction is not statistical; it is structural. If candidates can depend (directly or indirectly) on the gate’s decision, then self-reference yields diagonal constructions in which any total computable gate must fail, either by accepting a non-improvement or by rejecting (or missing) an available improvement. 1

papers.title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
papers.first_page: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research Yufa Zhou1,2,‡,† , Yichen Wang3 , Jiakun Fan1,4 , Ziqi Shu1 , Zhichao Liu1 , Anru R. Zhang2 , Neiwen Ling1,† , Zijun Wei1,† 1 ByteDance, 2 Duke University, 3 The University of Chicago, 4 Virginia Tech arXiv:2610.21055v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026 ‡ Project lead, † Corresponding authors Abstract Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor’s services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign’s full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other’s models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today’s agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research. “Instead of trying to produce a programme to simulate the adult mind, why not rather try to produce one which simulates the child’s? If this were then subjected to an appropriate course of education one would obtain the adult brain.” — Alan M. But how much of this gain re- flects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set? papers.title: Epi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research
papers.first_page: Épi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research Yue Huang1,2 Zhangchen Xu1,3 Xiaonan Luo1,2 Zheyuan Liu1,2 Lichi Li1 Yiping Wang3 Peiyang Song7 Eric Gabriel Ramos4 Enze Xie6 Olexandr Isayev7 Paul Liang8 Nouha Dziri9 Huan Sun10 Jianfeng Gao11 Ying Liu5 Misha Sra12 Xiangliang Zhang2 Alex Pentland8,13 Zichen Chen1,12,13 1 Bake AI 2 University of Notre Dame 3 University of Washington 4 Stevens Institute of Technology 5 Scale AI 6 NVIDIA 7 Carnegie Mellon University 8 MIT 9 Cohere Labs 10 11 12 13 arXiv:2610.24944v1 [cs.CL] 18 Oct 2026 The Ohio State University Microsoft UC Santa Barbara Stanford University Technical Report October 2026 Abstract We present Épi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. Épi combines persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to maintain research continuity, learn from experiments, and explore and revisit alternative approaches. Its experiments run across session boundaries, and a fixed verifier evaluates their outputs. Épi produced 120 record-setting results, comprising 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. These include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the n-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact dual certificates establish that the Cohn–Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Beyond numerical improvements, Épi gives a computer-assisted proof of Tuza’s conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We extend this research process to algorithmic coding with Épi-turbo, a lightweight configuration that develops executable solvers for tasks including vehicle routing, scheduling and production planning. On 30 FrontierOR tasks, Épi-turbo achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort. Épi is designed to support human understanding by connecting computational results to explicit methods and mathematical arguments that researchers can examine and build upon.  Blog § Results on GitHub 1 Introduction Autonomous research agents must conduct experiments, interpret results and revise their methods over many interactions. FunSearch and AlphaEvolve demonstrate how agents can combine code generation with executable evaluation to discover new programs and constructions (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). The AI Scientist-v2 extends automation to an experimental workflow (Yamada et al., 2025). When an investigation requires more work than one model session can support, however, the agent must manage three additional challenges. First, maintaining research continuity. Experiments and research decisions span multiple model sessions. To continue an investigation, the agent needs access to running jobs, code, intermediate results and reasons for earlier decisions. Kosmos maintains a shared research state, InternAgent-1.5 organizes long-horizon memory, and ScienceFlow archives recoverable execution states (Mitchener et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). These mechanisms preserve information across steps. As the history grows, the agent must also select what a bounded model context needs: the current experimental state, relevant lessons and reasons 1

papers.title: DuoDiscover: Scaling Autonomous Discovery Beyond the Evaluation Bottleneck
papers.first_page: 2026-10-12 DuoDiscover: Scaling Autonomous Discovery Beyond the Evaluation Bottleneck Shubham Agarwal*1,2 , Akshat Gupta*1,2 , Mike Heddes*1 , Dilara Soylu*1,3 , Rui Meng1 , Patrick Tser Jern Kon1 , Jiefeng Chen1 , Mert Cemri1,2 , Shu Liu2 , Abe Gonzalez1 , Akanksha Jain1 , Bhavana Dalvi Mishra1 , Linfeng Song1 , Vilobh Meshram1 , Xiangru Tang1 , Jinsung Yoon1 , Aditya Parameswaran2 , Ion Stoica2 , Vahab Mirrokni1 , Burak Gokturk1 , Parthasarathy Ranganathan1 , Tomas Pfister1 , Nanyun Peng†1 and Chun-Liang Li†1 1 Google 2 UC Berkeley 3 Stanford University * Equal contribution, ordered alphabetically. † Co-last authors. arXiv:2610.17184v1 [cs.CL] 12 Oct 2026 Evaluation has been central to advances in AI, and it is equally critical to autonomous discovery. Yet scaling autonomous discovery to real-world engineering challenges faces a fundamental bottleneck: the cost of evaluating progress. In real settings, a single true evaluation, such as a full benchmark or serving trace, can take hours, so a search can afford only a handful of true evaluations. We present DuoDiscover, a search system that jointly discovers what to optimize and how to evaluate progress efficiently, through three mechanisms. First, each worker in a fleet of coding agents co-discovers an optimization target and a fast, tailored proxy evaluator, which we call a yardstick. The agent then hill-climbs the yardstick rather than the true evaluation. Second, since search can exploit gaps between a yardstick and the true objective, fidelity tests continually recheck each yardstick’s ranking and invalidate any that drift. Third, the fleet is bottom-up, with no central decomposition of the problem. A lightweight orchestrator spawns and terminates agents, briefs running ones, and seeds new agents with others’ confirmed work. DuoDiscover enables autonomous optimization from software to chip architecture. We demonstrate DuoDiscover on two repository-level benchmarks and four GPU and TPU kernel suites covering hundreds of kernels. On SWE-fficiency, it doubles the average speedup of human experts. On SOL-Exec, it ranks first on 121 of 235 kernels and in the top three on 212. On the heavily optimized vLLM and SQLite engines, DuoDiscover achieves 1.92× and 1.38× gains over the base code. On a CPU microarchitecture optimization task with evaluations of up to 28 hours, DuoDiscover surpasses both AlphaEvolve-based ArchAgent v2 and the best human design, with 1.65× ArchAgent v2’s gain in 16.7 days versus more than 40 days, advancing the frontier of autonomous chip design. papers.title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery
papers.first_page: M ELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery Sizhe Tang1 , Zuyuan Zhang1 , Zeyu Fang1 , Tian Lan1 1 George Washington University Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce Meld, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a arXiv:2610.24454v1 [cs.AI] 17 Oct 2026 team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, Meld is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor. Author E-mails: s.tang1@gwu.edu Project Code: https://github.com/sizhe-tang/MELD-RSI Date: October 2026 1 Introduction Scientific discovery requires judiciously allocating a limited exploration/evaluation budget … me training (TTT) uses discovery feedback to adapt their research policies (Wang et al., 2026b; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026; Juneja et al., 2026). For a team of collaborative agents, each local research assignment determines both the team’s overall progress and the learning experience that shapes the team’s subsequent research strategy. Agent coordination in scientific discovery, such as focusing collective effort on promising research lineages while maintaining sufficient exploration, becomes part of the learning process rather than merely a scheduling mechanism. Existing approaches provide complementary capabilities. Tsaftaris S.Tsaftaris@ed.ac.uk Causality in Healthcare AI Hub (CHAI) School of Engineering, University of Edinburgh Abstract The success of autonomous research systems relies on the quality of the scientific hypotheses they generate. Recent studies report that human reviewers often rate LLM-generated ideas as more novel than those from human experts (Si et al., 2025; 2026; Jiang, 2026), raising hope that AI can accelerate scientific discovery. Yet it is unclear whether these models can do more than extend existing knowledge (Bao et al., 2026). Can LLMs drive genuine innovation by revealing new research directions, or are they limited to repeating and recombining what science already knows? This unresolved question lies at the heart of discussions about AI and the future of science. To address this, we distinguish two types of novelty: distance, which measures how far a hypothesis lies from existing work, and direction, which captures whether the hypothesis pursues new lines of inquiry beyond those already present. These two measures diverge sharply for LLM-generated work. We represent scientific papers in a shared conceptual space using a pretrained scientific-paper embedding model(Singh et al., 2023). Within this space, we embed 26.9 million human-authored papers across 1,325 research topics in six natural-science fields and 524,308 LLM-generated hypotheses from eight models. LLMs consistently generate ideas more distant from existing work than human-authored papers, up to 16% further when the LLM is given the papers farthest from the centre of the topic. However, LLM hypotheses have a 15–23% lower median ONS than published papers from the same topic. Thus, LLMs move further from what is already known, but remain within established directions. This pattern persists across changes in various configurations. As a result, LLMs excel at extending the frontier but the creation of new directions is still led by human scientists. ∗ Equal contribution. 1

Existing work uses the outcome of each evaluation to determine how the next candidate should be revised for performance improvement. However, a candidate often combines multi- ple design decisions, and its overall outcome alone does not reveal which decisions produced their expected effects, whether their required conditions were satisfied, or which decisions should be retained or revised. Inspired by ablation studies in the machine learning community, we propose DAGLoop to test the expected effect of a design decision by comparing implementations with and without that decision while preserving the other decisions it requires. Specifically, DAGLoop translates each design decision’s rationale into a testable expectation and pairs it with a targeted experiment, forming an experimental specification for assessing the expected effect under its required conditions. Using these specifications, we formulate ablation planning as the construction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from the candidate method’s design: nodes associate decisions with tests, and edges encode dependencies. The DAG specifies which decisions each experiment must retain and supports joint tests when an expected effect requires several decisions to act together. Outcomes are recorded with the tested decisions, expectations, and conditions to form structured research memory. This memory guides the agent in retaining experimentally supported decisions, revising unsupported ones, and plan- ning further experiments when the evidence is unresolved. Experiments on dozens of research tasks demonstrate substantial performance improvements achieved by DAGLoop across diverse executable research settings. Code and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/deng34567/DAGLoop. 1 I NTRODUCTION Improving a machine learning method requires repeated decisions about what to change, what to test, and how to interpret the result. Ayush Bansal1 Aldo Pareja2 Sean Klein1 Serge Didenko1 Artem Lukoianov1,3 1 2 3 Autolab AI Institute of Foundation Models MIT October 2026 arXiv:2610.22599v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026 Abstract Recent advances in AI make Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) increasingly plausible. Large Language Models (LLMs) can already propose, select, and run Machine Learning (ML) experiments. However, the space of possible design choices in ML is vast. An LLM that proposes an experiment needs a reliable intuition of whether it is worth running given the timing constraints of long training runs. In this work, we measure such intuition in current frontier LLMs by evaluating how accurately they predict the impact of self-generated ML experiment ideas before these are put into training runs. To this end, we construct a dataset of 288 LLM-proposed ideas on eight MLE-bench tasks. We then prompt five frontier LLMs (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3) to predict the impact of each idea and compare their predictions with the actual outcomes after training. We report four main findings. First, LLM predictions are substantially better than random chance but far from accurate: even the best model, Claude Opus 5.5, explains only half of the variance in outcomes (R2 = 0.49). Second, we notice that all tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of the changes. Third, prediction quality varies widely across tasks. Finally, the choice of the coding harness that actually implements the ideas has little effect on outcomes, and we find no evidence of self-preference. Higher reasoning settings and additional context lead to modest gains. Overall, our results show that current LLMs have useful but limited intuition about which ML ideas will work.
